complexity.explanation: Evaluating and rasterizing a single cubic Bézier spline segment requires computing cubic Bernstein polynomials and De Casteljau subdivision over bounded sub-pixel line segments, running in constant O(1) time and memory.

executionTrace.memoryDetail: Begins a new subpath anchored at initial endpoint P₀ (50, 180).
Evaluates cubic spline equation B(t) between P₀ and P₁ with control anchors CP₁ (100, 110) and CP₂ (200, 110).
Configures 4px stroke width and color token in active 2D context.
Tessellates the mathematical curve into linear micro-segments and blits anti-aliased fragments to the framebuffer.

pitfalls.title: Inverting the Canvas Y-Axis Direction
pitfalls.description: Unlike standard Cartesian graphs where Y points upward, Canvas screen coordinates have Y increasing downward. Adding height drags control points down, producing a sagging valley instead of an arched wave.
pitfalls.badSnippet:
// Adding height pushes control points downward into a sag
const cpY = startY + peakHeight;
pitfalls.goodSnippet:
// Subtracting height pulls control points upward toward top of canvas
const cpY = startY - peakHeight;

pitfalls.title: Discontinuous Spline Tangents at Joint Boundaries
pitfalls.description: When connecting multiple Bézier segments, placing control handles at mismatched angles creates non-differentiable sharp cusps (lacking C¹ continuity) at joint endpoints.

seniorInterviewTip: For smooth multi-segment curves, P_end, CP₂, and the next CP₁ must be collinear to satisfy C¹ continuity. If the tangent lengths are also equal, the curve satisfies C² continuity (curvature continuity), which is required in high-end vector engines and automotive CAD rendering.
